_comment: The closed verdict enum for every node type, and what each verdict must carry. Shape lives in verdict.schema.json; this file says which shape applies when, and which EDGE the verdict selects — graph.json says where that edge leads. A verdict that is not listed here does not exist; that is what 'closed enum' means.

tools._why: It cannot cross its own outgoing edge. commit is an edge, merge is an edge, and closing the issue is an edge — the rule the whole graph rests on stops being rhetorical exactly here.

reviewer._note: approve does not mean merge. It means this node found nothing verify cannot see. The gate is still ./verify, on the edge after this one.
reviewer._inputs_why: The diff, the criteria it is judged against, the charter, and what the gate already found. Nothing else — notably not the Builder's payload, which is where an argument for approval would travel.

tools._why: A judge that can edit what it is judging is not a judge. Note it cannot run ./verify either: the gate already ran on the edge behind it, and a Reviewer that re-runs the gate is judging its own rerun.
It files work; it does not do the work and it does not close it.

sweeper._note: Anything it finds becomes an issue, not a notification. A notification is something to ignore; an issue has a state.

tools._why: Anything it finds becomes an issue, not a notification.

human._note: A human node is a node like any other; the only difference is who fills in the verdict. Its verdict is the `value` of whichever option was chosen from the question that parked the token here, and the option's `edge` is the one crossed. So its enum is not fixed here — it is whatever the parking question offered.

launch._comment: How a node is invoked. Isolation is a property of the process: each node is a separate `claude -p` with a fresh context window, so the only question is what bytes the runner puts in. These lists are the contract; tests/test_manifest.py asserts the runner's argv against them.
launch._banned_why: --resume/--continue/--fork-session are the literal inherit-the-transcript flags; a node that resumes is not a node. --append-system-prompt leaves the default agent prompt underneath, with behaviours nobody chose or audited. The skip-permissions pair would make the tool policy advisory.
launch._required_why: --system-prompt-file replaces rather than appends (it is undocumented in --help but real, and validates the path: measured, not assumed). --strict-mcp-config because otherwise every ambient MCP server is live in every node — here Gmail, Drive, Calendar and Chrome, and a Reviewer that can send email is not a Reviewer.
launch._cwd_why: Measured, not assumed. Auto-memory is keyed by project path: a headless run inside /mnt/projects/control-plane receives the operator's MEMORY.md index verbatim, which is Builder-authored free text arriving in the Reviewer's context. --system-prompt does not close it and neither does --setting-sources ''; --bare does, but --bare cannot authenticate on an OAuth subscription ('Not logged in'), and nodes run on Claude Code rather than an API key. Changing cwd to the node's own worktree closes it.
launch._tools_comment: Deny by default: a tool absent from `allowed` is not granted, and `denied` names the ones that must never be granted even by a careless widening of the allowlist. The PreToolUse hook (bin/cp-guard) sits behind both, so a gap in one is not a gap in both. Allowlists are sub-tool scoped — Bash(git diff:*) grants exactly that, not Bash — which is what makes the policy enforceable rather than advisory.
launch._escalation_comment: ToolSearch, Task and Agent are denied at every node because they are the tools that grant other tools. A node that can spawn a subagent gets an agent with default tools, which is the whole policy bypassed in one call. Observed: a Reviewer asked to edit a file did not attempt Edit — it attempted ToolSearch to go and get Edit.
launch._readers_comment: Read-only filters are granted so a node can do ordinary work — piping a diff through head is not an escalation. The writers and interpreters beside them are denied explicitly: sed -i edits in place, awk and the interpreters run arbitrary code, and tee and xargs are writes wearing a filter's clothes. Granting neither was worse than it sounds: a Reviewer denied its own cp-verdict call reworded the finding until it got through.
launch._backend_why: Nodes run on Claude Code with the interactive session's own authentication, not on an API key: subscription usage rather than metered spend, and no second credential. Proven end to end — a Reviewer under the full flag set reviewed a real diff and emitted a valid verdict with no key present. This is why --bare is banned rather than merely unused: under --bare, auth is strictly ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or apiKeyHelper and OAuth is never read.
